item.title: The New Definition of LARPing
item.description:
Deception

The New Definition of LARPing

The internet slang "LARP" now goes well beyond its original meaning.

Posted August 5, 2026

Key points
  • LARPing originally arose in gaming when players impersonated characters for fun.
  • LARP has become Internet slang for faking some kind of identity, expertise, hobby, or lifestyle.
  • People LARP to get real-world attention, popularity, career advanacement, power, love, or money
  • LARPing can especially tough to maintain.
Source: Eugene Lisyuk / Pexels

Is "LARPing" playing some kind of role in your life?

There was the original gaming meaning of LARPing—Live-Action Role-Playing—which referred to dressing up in real life like Xena the Warrior Princess, Drizzt Do'Urden from Dungeons & Dragons, or some other fantasy character and then acting out what that character would normally do.

Then there's the new definition of LARPing that's been spreading on social media: It's when you fake some kind of identity, expertise, hobby, or lifestyle in order to get what you hope to be real attention, popularity, power, money, or even love.

The Original Meaning of LARPing

The term LARPing arose from role-playing games like Dungeons & Dragons, Pathfinder, Pokémon, Final Fantasy, and The Elder Scrolls that began as table-top games but eventually transitioned online as well. In such games, you are supposed to assume some type of identify—hence the word "role"—and play—hence the word "play"—that character throughout the game. It becomes "live-action" when you try to impersonate the character as much as possible—including donning a costume—while interacting with others in person.

This form of LARPing has become quite popular. People LARP for fun, to express themselves, to escape momentarily from reality, to bond with others, or to work together toward a mutual goal like a game-based quest. LARPing events occur throughout the world at gatherings like the ConQuest of Mythodea that every August brings around 10,000 players to a tent city in Hanover, Germany, to engage in a five-day "epic conflict."

A New Meaning of LARPing

The new type of LARPing is a totally different story. When someone accuses you of LARPing and you are not holding a mace or quarterstaff, that person is probably claiming that you are trying to fool others with a false image of yourself. It would be right to take that as an insult. One example of such LARPing is putting yourself forward as an expert in some subject like artificial intelligence when you don't actually have much deep knowledge or experience. Another example is flexing supposed wealth or power when there isn't any, like wearing expensive clothing that you can't afford or posing in a photo next to an expensive car that you don't own.

There's also acting as if you belong to some kind of profession or group when you really don't, such as pretending to be a doctor or to have graduated from a certain school. Then there's misrepresenting your physical appearance through the use of different angles, filters, editing software, make-up, plastic surgery, and other means to alter your facial features, skin tone, or body shape or size.

Here's a shocker: Social media is full of LARPing. Yes, there are plenty of people LARPing online and in real life in attempts to get ahead in their personal and professional lives and sell you stuff—including themselves; if you are looking to meet a LARPer on a dating app, you should have no problem finding one.

Why People LARP

LARPing can arise from insecurity—feeling deep down that you don't really believe that you can't get what you want by simply being yourself. Laziness can lead to LARPing too—an attempt to circumvent hard work, effort, and time in the "fake it until you make it" vein. You may also LARP because you want to manipulate others: "Fool them once...hey. that worked!"

Any of the above could be more natural and thus more excusable when you are still quite young, before you may have formed a sense of self and grown to be more comfortable in your own skin. So if a five-year-old, for example, tells you that he's "king of the world" and "the CEO of Microgoogle," you don't necessarily have to burst his bubble and call him a liar. A 30-year-old saying something similar is a different story. At some point you should be old enough to know better.

The Risks of LARPing

When any part of your life is built on a false and shaky foundation, your world can become a house of cards that can come crashing down once a falsehood gets exposed. Therefore, you can spend an enormous amount of time, effort, and stress to protect this house and maintain such false pretenses. And in the process, you may keep adding deceptions until you become unrecognizable to yourself. Just look at what happened to George Santos and Elizabeth Holmes.

If you ever feel the urge to LARP, you may want to ask yourself why you feel the need to play a role. If you are feeling insecure, why is this the case? Why not instead cherish who you are, rely on your own unique abilities, and do the hard work needed to get what you want? Truly earning something and being yourself will bring more satisfaction.

How To Deal With LARPing

If you encounter someone who's LARPing, should you call them out publicly? If it's someone close to you whom you care about, maybe ask that person in a private setting why they are presenting such an image. That person may need help seeing what their real self has to offer and what the benefits of being of being more authentic may be.

item.title: Antidepressants and Suicide Risk
item.description:
Suicide

Antidepressants and Suicide Risk

Why early treatment requires careful monitoring, not fear.

Posted August 5, 2026

Key points
  • Suicide reports show associations, not proof that antidepressants caused the events.
  • Children, adolescents, and older adults may require closer monitoring after starting treatment.
  • Underreporting may substantially underestimate the true number of serious adverse events.
Source: Stormseeker / Unsplash

Whether antidepressants can trigger suicidal thoughts in some patients remains one of the most controversial questions in psychopharmacology. Clinical trials offer only part of the answer because they rarely include people with active suicidal ideation.

To address this gap, a study published in Pharmaceuticals analyzed adverse event reports from EudraVigilance, the European Medicines Agency's pharmacovigilance database, covering six widely prescribed antidepressants between 2001 and 2024.

Pharmacovigilance data cannot establish causation. A reported suicide does not mean the drug caused it, only that a possible link was suspected and reported. Even so, these reports can reveal important safety signals.

The weight of psychiatric adverse events

The study's broadest finding concerns the share of psychiatric reactions within the total pool of reported adverse events. Across the six drugs, that share ranged from 33.9% to 38.2%. Roughly one in three reported that adverse events involved psychiatric symptoms.

Two drugs stood out for different reasons. Venlafaxine led in absolute numbers, with 13,134 psychiatric reports, likely reflecting both its volume of use and its pharmacological profile as an SNRI. Duloxetine, meanwhile, had the highest relative share, 38.2% of all its reports.

Completed suicide, attempt, and ideation: Why the categories matter

The study analyzed five separate outcomes: completed suicide, suicidal behavior, suicidal ideation, suicide attempt, and suspected suicide. Looking at them individually revealed patterns that would have been missed if they had been grouped into a single category.

Venlafaxine had the highest number of completed suicides (1,635), followed by citalopram (1,359), fluoxetine (1,296), and duloxetine (1,070). However, when completed suicides were analyzed as a proportion of each drug's total adverse event reports, citalopram and fluoxetine ranked highest at 6%, while venlafaxine dropped to 4%.

Duloxetine stood out for a different reason. It generated the highest number of reports of suicidal behavior and suicidal ideation, but fewer completed suicides than venlafaxine, citalopram, and fluoxetine. However, the paper contains an inconsistency. While the text states that duloxetine had the lowest number of completed suicides among the six drugs, the accompanying table identifies escitalopram as the lowest, with 880 cases compared with duloxetine's 1,070.

Interpretation is further limited because nearly 3,900 duloxetine reports do not record the final outcome. Without knowing whether those patients survived, died, or recovered, it is impossible to determine whether duloxetine truly follows a different pattern or whether the apparent difference simply reflects incomplete reporting.

Gender, a consistent pattern with an uncertain cause

Across all six drugs, women reported more adverse events than men. The gap was widest for duloxetine, where 67% of reports came from women, and for sertraline, at 61.3%.

The study can't isolate why, and it's upfront about that limitation. Factors include:

  • Pharmacokinetic differences, including slower drug clearance in women for certain compounds
  • Hormonal and body composition differences
  • Reporting bias, since women seek medical care and report symptoms more often than men

Without data on how many women versus men actually use each drug, there's no way to know how much of this pattern reflects genuine biological risk and how much simply reflects who's more likely to report.

Age, the finding that should worry clinicians most

As expected, the 18 to 64 age group accounted for the highest number of suicide attempts across all six drugs.

The more delicate finding sits in the 0 to 17 age group. Here, the drug-by-drug distribution shifts considerably. Sertraline led, accounting for 21.8% of all suicide attempts reported for that drug, followed by fluoxetine (19.3%) and escitalopram (14.7%). Duloxetine had the smallest share in this age group, 2.1%, which likely reflects its much more limited pediatric use.

Fluoxetine remains, in the literature, one of the best studied and safest options for children and adolescents, with escitalopram as an alternative when fluoxetine isn't well tolerated. What the numbers suggest instead is that even among the drugs considered safest for this population, close monitoring during the first weeks of treatment remains essential.

Among patients aged 65 to 85, duloxetine and venlafaxine led in suicide attempts, a finding the authors attribute to the mechanism of action of these two drugs, which act on both serotonin and norepinephrine simultaneously, producing a more complex pharmacological profile than pure SSRIs.

Underreporting changes the scale of the problem

The study's most uncomfortable point may not be the numbers it presents, but what they likely fail to capture.

The pharmacovigilance literature is fairly consistent in estimating that only 6% to 10% of real adverse events ever get reported to official systems. A European review cited by the authors put the median underreporting rate among healthcare professionals at 94%.

Working from that assumption, the researchers built a worst-case scenario, assuming only 6% of real events are actually captured. Under that assumption, the estimated number of completed suicides linked to venlafaxine would jump from 1,635 reported cases to 27,250. Total psychiatric reactions across the six drugs would exceed 1 million reports.

These figures are speculative by design, and the authors themselves frame the scenario as an exercise, not a confirmed estimate. It shows that the real scale of the problem could be an order of magnitude larger than what shows up in official databases.

What this means for clinical practice

No pharmacovigilance dataset, however robust, replaces individualized clinical judgment. Even so, the findings point to several practical implications:

  • The period of highest vulnerability remains treatment initiation, when a patient's physical energy tends to improve before mood does, opening a window where the capacity to act outpaces emotional recovery
  • Children, adolescents, and older adults deserve closer monitoring protocols, given the distinct risk profile observed at each end of the age spectrum
  • Pharmacovigilance systems need mandatory fields for the final outcome of reported events, since missing that information undermines much of the analytical value of the data collected

For anyone already on an antidepressant or considering starting one, the practical takeaway isn't alarm, but active vigilance. Reporting mood changes, unusual thoughts, or worsening symptoms to a physician, especially in the first few weeks, remains the most effective tool available for reducing risk while still pursuing the therapeutic benefit these medications, for most patients, genuinely provide.

If you or someone you love is contemplating suicide, seek help immediately. For help 24/7 dial 988 for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, or reach out to the Crisis Text Line by texting TALK to 741741. To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: "You're a Psychologist. You Know..."
item.description:
Intuition

"You're a Psychologist. You Know..."

What goes wrong when intuition borrows the authority of science.

Posted August 5, 2026

Key points
  • Many of us believe our folk theories about people are not just true, but scientifically backed.
  • We overestimate how well we understand minds—until we are asked to actually explain them.
  • Real expertise brings humility: the more we learn about the mind, the more we see what we don't know.

I have spent more than three decades studying, teaching, researching, mentoring, and practicing psychology. One phrase has followed me everywhere—dinner parties, clinics, classrooms, even the grocery store:

"You're a psychologist. You know..."

What comes next is always interesting. It is rarely psychology. Sometimes it is folk wisdom; sometimes a stereotype dressed as insight; sometimes—the part that fascinates me most—something scientific psychology rejected decades ago. It is said with complete confidence, as though my decades of study had merely been catching up to what everyone already knows. And the phrase contains a quiet trap: Because psychology itself has been enlisted as their witness, disagreeing with them doesn't sound like expertise but like disagreeing with science. There is a paradox folded inside it, too: The phrase recognizes expertise in the very act of erasing it. My colleagues report the same experience.

Now, before this sounds like a complaint, an admission: I do exactly the same thing. I have confidently explained inflation to economists and nutrition to physicians. This is not a story about annoying laypeople. It is a story about a cognitive illusion all of us share—one my field simply makes visible to me.

The Illusion of Knowing

The phrase troubles me not because people are wrong—being wrong is universal—but because of the claim hidden inside it. The speaker is asserting that their intuition is what the science says; that what they absorbed from culture, upbringing, social media, and movies is equivalent to knowledge developed through systematic observation, measurement, testing, replication, and correction.

Psychology invites this appropriation more than most fields because everyone has a mind. No one believes that living in buildings makes them a structural engineer. But having emotions, relationships, children, and disappointments can feel like having studied human behavior. Personal experience supplies psychological data, not psychological knowledge.

Psychology has a name for the underlying mechanism: the illusion of explanatory depth. People believe they understand how things work far better than they do; for example, they're confident they know how a zipper works until they're asked to draw one (Rozenblit & Keil, 2002). Minds invite the illusion even more. We often lack reliable access even to our own mental processes, confidently reporting reasons for our behavior that were not the causes (Nisbett & Wilson, 1977). If we misread the one mind we occupy, our confidence about everyone else's deserves suspicion.

"I Just Need Two Minutes"

There is a second phrase I hear even more often, delivered with pride: "I'm a good psychologist myself. I just need two minutes: One look at someone, and I know who they are."

Let me be honest about what the evidence shows. First impressions are not worthless: Research on "thin slices" suggests that brief observations can sometimes predict specific, narrowly defined outcomes with modest accuracy (Ambady & Rosenthal, 1992). But predicting a limited outcome is a very long way from knowing who someone is. No psychological training allows us to look at another person and reliably apprehend their character, motives, history, and likely behavior as a whole.

Everyday life supplies an equally sobering counterexample. Spend a day in family court and you will hear people married for 20, 30, or 40 years—people who shared beds, children, finances, illnesses, and dreams—say, with genuine bewilderment, "I don't know who this person is. How did I not see it?" They had thousands of chances to "read" each other, and still they were surprised. If human beings could reliably know one another after a glance or a two-minute conversation, we would not so regularly be shocked by partners, friends, and family members we have known for years. But we are shocked constantly.

The two-minute fantasy is not harmless. It licenses snap judgments, converts bias into "instinct"—and, worse, ends curiosity. It resembles what clinicians call premature closure: Once you have decided who someone is, you stop asking. The judgment is never revised, because it was never held as a judgment. It was held as knowledge.

The Paradox of Expertise

Here is the pattern underneath it all: intuition mistaken for expertise, confidence mistaken for accuracy, personal impression presented as scientific conclusion. Fragments from a TED talk, a self-help book, or a podcast are absorbed and promoted into "what psychology says." Research on self-assessment points to the structure underneath: the less knowledge people have in a domain, the less equipped they are to recognize what they are missing (Kruger & Dunning, 1999). Certainty, it turns out, is cheapest exactly where knowledge is thinnest.

And so, after 30 years, here is what I actually know. I cannot know you in two minutes; I barely begin to know you in two years. I am often wrong. My training does not prevent error; it helps me recognize and correct it sooner. What I know came from study, not instinct, and it remains permanently incomplete. The paradox of expertise is that those who know the most are often the most aware of their limits, while those with less knowledge may be less able to recognize what they are missing. Psychological training, in the end, does not give us the power to see through people. It gives us better methods for asking questions, testing interpretations, distinguishing evidence from intuition, and recognizing how easily we may be wrong.

A Gentle Request

So here is my request, offered warmly, to anyone who has ever begun a conversation with "You're a psychologist. You know..."

Your interest in the human mind is wonderful; it is the most fascinating subject there is. Ask me what the research actually says; I love the question. But telling me what I know is a different act. The same courtesy extends beyond my profession—to the economist, the physician, the teacher, the engineer—everyone whose decades of study get summarized back to them with confidence.

The next time any of us feels that comfortable certainty rising—about a field, or about a person—there is a more interesting move available: the pause. Consider the possibility of being wrong. Consider that the person in front of you is more complicated than your first reading—and more interesting for it. That pause, that small tolerated uncertainty, is where real wisdom begins.

item.title: How to Connect with Adopted and Foster Children
item.description:
Adverse Childhood Experiences

How to Connect with Adopted and Foster Children

Their hidden wounds can frustrate the most well-intentioned caregivers.

Posted August 5, 2026

Key points
  • “Children from hard places” bring challenges that most adoptive and foster parents are ill-equipped to handle.
  • Understanding these challenges helps distressed caregivers and those contemplating adopting or foster care.
  • Key principles and skills help all parents, those working with at-risk children, and the children themselves.

This post is part of a series on adverse childhood experiences. Read the other parts here.

Adopted or foster children come with challenging experiences. All have been separated from their biological parents. Many had biological mothers who experienced prenatal distress, heavy drinking, or other difficulties. Others have experienced neglect or abuse, or have witnessed domestic violence. Though they might appear normal outwardly, many will show:

  • Attachment problems, such as refusing affection
  • Impaired neurological development (dysregulated stress hormones damage the brain)
  • Social, learning, and or attention difficulties
  • Heightened sensitivity to unfamiliar sensory stimuli, such as sights, sounds, smells, tastes, or being touched (neglected children deprived of normal sensory stimuli can be overwhelmed by new sensations, as can traumatized children who are fearful and distrustful)
  • Rage, tantrums, aggression, and hyperactivity (What might appear to be defiance is often the child’s inability to regulate a hypervigilant nervous system)
  • Shame, withdrawal, numbing, and other trauma symptoms

Playing Catch Up

For these fragile children, caregivers must not only provide love, safety, and structure, but also patiently help them heal and satisfy their earliest unmet needs. Psychologist Karyn Purvis and colleagues have written a critically important resource, The Connected Child, which provides needed principles and skills for adoptive and foster parents, all parents, teachers, and anyone who works with children with troubled backgrounds.

Loving Discipline

At-risk children need to know that their caregivers are strong and love them enough to guide and teach them how to behave in society. However, sending adopted or foster children to their room, shaming, or angry discipline often exacerbates their feelings of isolation and creates resentment. Instead, Purvis suggests bringing the child to a think-it-over spot with the caregiver close by. The misbehavior becomes an opportunity to retrain. Some examples:

  • If a child angrily strikes another child, the caregiver can say, “Sit right here. I’ll be close by. Think about what you did wrong and how you can do it right. When you’re ready to use your words and tell me about what you did, say, ‘Ready,’ and I’ll come.” When the child is ready, the caregiver gets to the child’s eye level, makes eye contact, extends hands palm up, asks for the child’s hands, and holds them gently. The child describes what he did wrong. The caregiver might assist, perhaps explaining, “People are not for hurting.” Then the caregiver asks, “How can you do it right?” If the child comes up blank, walk arm in arm to the scene of the crime, correctly play out the scene, then lavishly praise the child for his efforts.
  • If the child says, “I hate you,” the parent quickly says, “Hold it. It’s not okay for you to talk to me with those kinds of words.” The caregiver kneels to eye level, gently takes the child’s hands, and says, “Tell me what you need and with respect.” Gently touching just under the child’s chin, the caregiver says, “Let me see those eyes. I love to see those eyes. Sweetheart, you can say anything you need to say to me. If you think I’m being mean, you can say that; just say it with respect. Tell me what you need.” Perhaps the child says, “I don’t want to go to bed yet.” And the caregiver compliments, “Good using words.”
  • The caregiver asks, “Are you angry? What are you angry about? Use your words and tell me.” Then compliment, “Great telling me.” If the child is shut down, the caregiver might draw the child in and ask, “Where in the body do you feel it? What color describes the anger?”
  • The caregiver teaches the child to ask for what she wants respectfully, and to accept “no.” (“Whoa, if you ask disrespectfully, the answer will always be ‘no.’ If you ask respectfully, the answer might be yes or no. Let’s try asking again with respect.” For example, a child who was deprived of food and hoards food asks for a snack. The caregiver, respecting the child’s needs while maintaining authority, replies, “Yes, you might have this snack bar and eat it right after supper. Would you like it right beside your plate or in your pocket until dinner is over?”

Other Principles and Strategies

  • Balance structure and nurturing. Build close connection through warm interactions and gentle correcting to help the child master new skills. (“I love you, and I want to help you get this right.”) Love disarms the fear response. However, overcoming ingrained distrust and forming close connections can take a long time.
  • Medications, while sometimes helping to reduce symptom severity, cannot alone overcome the full range of adjustment issues in the adopted or foster child. The caregiver, however, is continually with the child and able to coach and build attachment bonds, sometimes with the help of skilled psychotherapy.
  • Help children prepare for change. Alert the child to upcoming activities (“In 10 minutes we’ll put toys away and come to dinner.”)
  • Give limited choices, as appropriate. (“Would you like to take a nap or just rest quietly?”)
  • Manage sensory stimuli. Decorate simply and subtly. Minimize air fresheners. Minimize loud voices and loud media sounds. Avoid too many toys and clutter.
  • Be approachable. Rather than giving toys that encourage isolation, give games or toys that encourage playing together. Try games you can enjoy together, such as Simon Says, which teaches listening and obedience.
  • Don’t dictate the child’s story (Instead of "Your mother loved you and wanted to keep you, and was so loving,” try “I don’t know much about your mother and what she was going through. What do you think she felt when she gave you up?”)
  • Encourage the distractible child to focus (“Barry, what is the task I asked you to do? Focus and complete your task.”)

The authors offer additional principles and skills for dealing with defiance, playing games that connect, teaching children good ways to manage anger, teaching the child to respectfully ask for a compromise (which the caregiver defines), and more. Although the process of healing and guiding children from troubled backgrounds to become responsible and enjoyable individuals can take years, these principles and skills can turn moments of anguish into more moments of delight.

item.title: The Hidden Mistake Parents Make When Praising Their Children
item.description:
Parenting

The Hidden Mistake Parents Make When Praising Their Children

How your words shape resilience, confidence, and lifelong motivation.

Posted August 5, 2026

Key points
  • The science behind the praise that helps children thrive under pressure.
  • Effort-based praise helps children develop resilience and persistence.
  • Specific feedback is more powerful than labels like "smart" or "gifted."

Most parents want their children to feel confident, capable, and loved. Naturally, we praise them. We celebrate good grades, soccer goals, artwork taped to the refrigerator, and the first successful trip to the potty.

But here’s something many parents never consider: Not all praise is equally helpful.

In fact, some forms of praise may unintentionally undermine confidence, increase fear of failure, or reduce a child’s intrinsic motivation. The good news? A few simple changes in how you praise your child can have lasting effects on emotional development and behavior.

Praise Should Tell Children What They Did Right

Imagine your child shares a favorite toy with a sibling. Many parents instinctively respond with, “Good job!” or “I’m proud of you!” While well-intended, those words don’t teach the child what behavior deserves repeating.

Instead, try something more specific: “I noticed you shared your blocks with your brother even though you were still playing with them. That was incredibly kind.”

Specific praise helps children connect your approval to concrete behavior. Rather than wondering what earned the praise, they learn exactly which actions reflect kindness, responsibility, persistence, or self-control. Specificity turns praise into a teaching tool.

Timing Matters More Than Parents Realize

Children—especially younger ones—learn best when feedback follows closely behind the behavior. When your preschooler remembers to put dirty clothes in the laundry basket or your elementary-school child starts homework without reminders, acknowledge it while the moment is still fresh. Immediate praise strengthens the connection between behavior and positive reinforcement.

As new habits become established, parents can gradually become less frequent with praise. Children eventually internalize these behaviors, allowing motivation to shift from external encouragement to internal satisfaction.

Focus on Effort, Not Talent

One of the most powerful lessons psychology has taught us is that children benefit from believing abilities can grow. Compare these two statements: “You’re so smart.” Versus “You worked really hard studying for that test." The first praises an identity. The second praises effort.

Children who repeatedly hear effort-based praise are more likely to embrace challenges, recover from setbacks, and believe improvement comes through practice rather than fixed ability. This approach helps cultivate what psychologists call a growth mindset—the belief that skills develop through persistence and learning rather than being predetermined.

Be Genuine

Children are remarkably skilled at detecting insincerity. If praise feels exaggerated or disconnected from reality, it loses credibility. Telling a child they’re “the best artist in the world” or “the smartest kid ever” may sound encouraging, but these sweeping statements often create unnecessary pressure.

article continues after advertisement

Instead, focus on authentic observations: “I love how much detail you added to your drawing.” “You stayed patient even when that puzzle became frustrating.” Genuine praise communicates that you are paying attention—not simply offering compliments out of habit.

When Praise Becomes Too Much

Many parents worry they don’t praise their children enough. Ironically, some children experience the opposite problem. Overpraising occurs when children receive excessive, vague, or inflated praise regardless of effort or accomplishment. When every drawing is “amazing,” every performance is “perfect,” and every accomplishment is treated as extraordinary, children may begin questioning whether the praise is sincere.

Some become fearful of making mistakes because they’ve developed an image they feel obligated to maintain. Others begin expecting constant recognition simply for participating. Neither outcome prepares children well for adulthood.

Healthy confidence develops from mastering challenges—not from hearing that everything they do is exceptional.

Praise Changes as Children Grow

The type of praise children need evolves with age. Toddlers often benefit from immediate praise while learning new behaviors like potty training, sharing, or cleaning up toys. School-aged children begin developing internal motivation, so praise becomes less about encouraging routine behaviors and more about recognizing perseverance, responsibility, kindness, and problem-solving.

Teenagers still need encouragement—but they often respond better when parents acknowledge character rather than controlling behavior. Instead of saying: “I’m proud of you for getting an A.” Try: “I noticed how consistently you studied this week. Your dedication really paid off.”

This subtle shift reinforces values that remain important long after report cards disappear.

One Powerful Addition: Gratitude

Some of the most meaningful conversations between parents and children combine praise with gratitude.

Imagine your child surprises you with a handmade card. Rather than simply saying, “Good job,” you might say: “You put so much thought into making this. Thank you for thinking of me. I feel incredibly lucky to be your parent.” Notice that the praise focuses on the child’s effort, while the gratitude expresses appreciation for the relationship itself.

article continues after advertisement

Children need to know they are loved for who they are—not only for what they accomplish. That distinction can strengthen emotional security in profound ways.

The Goal Isn’t Perfect Parenting

No parent gets this right every time. Every family occasionally blurts out a quick “Great job!” while rushing out the door. That’s okay. Effective parenting isn’t about perfection. It’s about being intentional more often than not.

When praise is specific, sincere, focused on effort, and delivered with warmth, it becomes far more than encouragement. It becomes one of the most powerful tools we have for raising resilient, confident, emotionally healthy children.
